HOT COPPER

By: Nicky Troll | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa is being unplugged. We expose a shadow industry of large-scale copper heists where syndicates, smugglers and silent buyers strip the nation for profit.

Unique Selling Point:
- a crime trend we've reported on before has morphed
- tension in armed escourts
- action in a raid


Summary:
LOGLINE
Copper is the lifeblood of South Africa’s infrastructure and criminals are ripping it out. This we know, this we’ve covered. But the crime trend has morphed, from live power cables and rail lines to a next level large scale criminal operations targeting cargo trucks, foundries and warehouses.


Further information:
PITCH
What was once petty scrap crime is now a million-rand black market feeding local syndicates and the global demand as copper theft takes on a new modus operandi. It’s not about targeting the low level thieves stealing bit by bit, it’s about closing the black market that’s honed in on big quantity thefts. This lucrative industry is now forced to have armed escorts protecting their loads in transit as syndicates shift their sights.

HOW TO TELL IT
We get the inside track from one of SA leading investigative companies piecing together the illicit trade in copper. They’ve got footage and rare insights into a market that has become a vicious cycle with some of the very targets, becoming the buyers. Stolen copper is often bought back by dodgy smelting facilities, getting in black market stock at a dramatically reduced price from the criminals that steal it.

ELEMENTS
RIDE-ALONG – THE TENSION
We ride with private security teams protecting copper shipments staking out dangerous routes. We unpack the transit chain, how stolen copper moves from pylons and cable trenches to the black market, and eventually overseas, despite export bans.

EXPERTISE – THE INSIGHT
We’ll speak to specialist private investigators and insurers covering copper cargo worth millions, explore the threads leading to a speculative but highly plausible export economy, where stolen copper is melted, disguised, and shipped out despite official bans.

FORENSICS – THE TECH
The investigations include a CSI styled element - they recover fragments of cut cable, trace tool marks, lift fingerprints off truck doors, and map syndicate movements through their informer networks.

RAID – THE ACTION
We tag along with a team of investigators as they hit suspect smelters in search of hot copper.

THE IMPACT
From street-level theft to export, this crime trend is halting train networks, plunging communities into darkness, and crippling vital infrastructure.

It’s not just copper that’s being stolen, it’s sabotage. It’s about national stability. Copper powers everything and right now, South Africa is being unplugged. This takes the viewer on a raw, investigative dive into the country’s illicit copper trade.

KEY THEMES
• The Rise of Copper Theft: What’s driving demand?
• Hot Cargo: How copper is hijacked in transit, and what security teams are up against
• Infrastructure Under Attack: Real-time impact on electricity, transport, and telecoms
• Insured Losses, Uncounted Costs: The economics of copper theft
• Where It Goes: Speculation and intelligence on export markets and supply chains

ADDITIONAL CONTEXT | FIGURES FROM EXISTING RESEARCH DOCS
Approximately 150 000 tonnes of copper scrap is legally traded in South Africa each year,
with a value of over R10 billion. Most is sold on the local market, with a smaller percentage,
approximately 13%, exported to other countries. However, some experts believe this
figure may be underestimated, due to industrial-scale under-invoicing and mislabelling.

Stolen copper smuggled by port leaves the country in containers that are either mislabelled or have
false documentation. In some cases, scrap copper is labelled as raw copper. This practice, which
involves customs fraud, appears to be common both in the smuggling of stolen copper and in the
export of scrap copper by some legitimate dealers. In other cases, illegal scrap copper is mislabelled
as non-metal goods, such as textiles, and then exported under the corresponding codes


SHIFT FROM EXPORTING SCRAP COPPER TO RAW COPPER – POSSIBLY STOLEN
The 2022 Trade and Industrial Policies Strategies report also points to a situation where, according to SARS figures, South Africa ‘now exports more raw copper than it produces and imports, and
four times more than the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy reports’.

With regard to stolen copper, there are no precise estimates of how much is traded, partly because
some is laundered back into the legal market, making it untraceable. However, it appears more is
exported than in the legal trade.

INTERNATIONAL MARKET
n 2021, China accounted for about 85% of all scrap metal exported from South Africa. 81 This was
followed by Germany (3.24%) and India (3.21%). Other countries or regions importing South African
scrap copper include Hong Kong SAR (China), the Netherlands, Korea, Belgium, Malaysia, Botswana
and Lesotho

THE MONEY
A private investigator source has explained that a container used for export through the ports can typically hold about 24 000 kilograms of scrap copper. If it is bought at R70 per kilogram (half the current legal price) but sold at the full price of R140 per kilogram, the profit on a single container is R1.7 million

The general price for scrap copper wiring ranges from R20 to R60 per kilogram.46 However, the value of stolen copper is in the lower range, usually between R15 and R20 per kilogram. After the copper has been recycled and processed, the selling price can increase to between R140 and R160 per kilogram.

FINAL SCRIPT | HOT COPPER

OPEN WITH CCTV FOOTAGE

[GOVAN]: This is CCTV footage of a copper heist in motion.

These men have taken over a truck stop. The target: R6 million of raw copper.

PAUSE…

[GOVAN]: Copper Theft is not a new crime trend.

UPSOUND: Suspects on Foot, we’re in pursuit.

UPSOUND: CB 2020 MAC: You’re running an operation here.

[GOVAN]: We’ve exposed the cable thieve and the shady scrapyards buying it up bit by bit.

This is not that story. The crime trend has evolved.

LINKS: This is orange gold. It's a high value metal, but stealing it in these quantities bit by bit isn't a big score. That's why syndicates are heisting tons at a time.

NEW CCTV HEIST FOOTAGE

[GOVAN]: Criminal operations target cargo trucks, foundries and warehouses in search of copper.

[MISHCA]: The illegal trade in copper has become one of the most lucrative and well organized illicit markets within South Africa.

[GOVAN]: It’s a shadow industry of massive copper heists with syndicates, smugglers and silent buyers all feeding into global demand.

[GOVAN]: Driven by the green energy transition, electric cars, and the world’s shift to digital. And the higher the world’s appetite , the more thieves are stepping up to feed it.

Mishca Pieterse is an Intelligence Co-ordinator.

[MISHCA]: With the copper demand going up in the recent year, we've maybe seen 5 or 6 in the past 12 months, which are major copper robberies, which we've seen a large amount of tonnage taken.

[GOVAN]: So this is what the syndicates are after. It's 34 tonnes of nearly pure copper worth over 6 million rand. And unfortunately, it's a moving target.

[GOVAN]: This footage is from a foundry under attack - sixteen robbers, five hours, a hundred and twenty tonnes of copper.

They bring in their own forklift drivers and five of their own superlink trucks. In one hit, eighteen million rands’ worth is gone.

[MICHIEL]: If there's a willing buyer, there's a guy who's willing to steal it and to make money from the business.

[GOVAN]: Michiel Brand runs armed escorts protecting high-value metal shipments from Botswana and Zimbabwe into South Africa.

[GOVAN]: How many copper trucks to escort per day?
[MICHIEL]: We personally, our company it can be anything from 50 to 70 trucks a day.
[GOVAN]: If you're a criminal this is a gold mine.
[MICHIEL]: It is, a very lucrative one.

[GOVAN]: At around R170 a kilo, a single ton is worth R170 000 - making every load a massive score.

[MISHCA]: If the copper is non-traceable, they can get 100% of that market value. If however it is traceable and it is what we call hot copper, then obviously the syndicates would settle for between 70 to 90% of the copper’s value.

[GOVAN]: Legitimate raw copper usually carries a signature: markings, or a shape forged by the original smelter. When it’s stolen, it gets reworked. The hot copper’s shape is changed to hide its criminal origin.

Think of it as copper laundering.

Roy Robertson heads one of the country’s leading copper-theft investigation firms.

[ROY]: The problem is, it goes to the metal trader they will melt it down into a blister block, which is now a so-called semi-finished product.

[GOVAN]: Once it’s been smelted down, it’s often destined for an international market.

[ROY]: There’s hardly any control of what's leaving the country in terms of inspection at the ports.

[GOVAN]: By the time it gets into a container, you'd never know it was stolen. It's been relabelled, and it's being shipped out. And overseas buyers don't ask questions. They just pay.

[GOVAN]: The hunt for copper never stops - they’ll clone security vehicles and forge paperwork to move product, and the next score could be anywhere, even inside a guarded truck stop.

This Gauteng Truckstop owner asked for his identity to be hidden to protect his business.

His yard is a known safe zone for high-value cargo. But earlier this year, that security didn’t matter – a syndicate infiltrated his truckstop around midnight.

[TRUCK STOP OWNER]: Highly, highly organized. They didn't decide to do this job a day before.

CCTV FOOTAGE

[TRUCK STOP OWNER]: There were four hidden guys inside their truck, which we did not see - they all four were armed. Every single facet of our business, they knew exactly what was going on.

[MISHCA]: It's a very deliberate and decisive attack. It's 15 to 20 people they know exactly where they're going, who they're looking for, how many people are on shift, where to keep them, where the panic buttons are, from there it's just rounding up the copper.

[GOVAN]: Once the four robbers secure the yard, their own trucks and back up arrive.

[TRUCK STOP OWNER]: Another vehicle came into the one gate, 20 guys came lock, stock and barrel AK 47s, the works. Then the site was basically all in their hands.

[GOVAN]: They gather around to get their weapons. Over the next four hours, they systematically reload 34 tonnes of copper worth about R6 million.

The robbers act as a unit, but with clearly designated tasks.

[MISHCA]: It's for deniability so that if you catch the foot soldiers, the syndicate can continue to operate. It's very premeditated and it's incredibly well set up.

[GOVAN]: Even in hijacking scenarios, these copper syndicates operate with military precision.

[MISHCA]: Those are high threat heists, where they would pull or coerce the truck onto the side with the threat of large rifles, large firearms, and then offload the copper. The alternative also is if you don't want that amount of violence, but you want to get the same end result, they would use law enforcement, branded vehicles and uniforms.

VISUAL GAP

[MICHIEL]: Usually the last truck in, in a convoy were targeted, and then a traffic cop or a police officer or someone that resembles one with a marked vehicle would pull over the vehicle.
[GOVAN]: They pulled over by the police?
[MICHIEL]: Pulled over by the police …
[GOVAN]: Is it real police? What do you think?
[MICHIEL]: It is a real police. It's a real police.

[GOVAN]: When you’re up against criminals and possibly law enforcement, you need to catch them in the act.

[ROY]: We installed a gas hawk camera on it, that will detect you about 30km at night, the infrared camera. You have to invest, otherwise, the crooks are a step ahead of you.

VO : This footage captures the takedown of a copper hijacking crew.

[ROY]: The helicopter could guide us exactly where they are. And then we managed to arrest all of them and we recovered all the goods as well.

[GOVAN]: The tech is built for the hunt.

CHOPPER TAKE OFF.

[SUB KEVIN]: We can get an all around picture of a scene. And also we can lock on or focus on a target so there’s no chance of escaping.
[SUB GOVAN]: So, tell me what this camera can do?
[SUB KEVIN]: In terms of its zoom capabilities it will auto detect a person from up to 5 to 10 kilometers away. We can pick up a vehicle and follow a vehicle from up to 15 to 20 kilometers away.

[GOVAN]: Investigators also try to kill the market by targeting the receivers of hot copper.

We’re joining an operation led by Johan Kritzinger, a private investigator specialising in copper theft cases. Today’s target - a Gauteng foundry, has been on the team’s radar before.

UPSOUND BRIEFING
[JOHAN]: Everybody here knows about this foundry - we had run-ins with this foundry in the past.

MUSIC BEAT

[GOVAN]: This team keeps an eye on smelters suspected of buying directly from the thieves and reworking it.

This year, they’ve hit seven foundries, retrieving stolen material every time.

[JOHAN]: And as we hit the place, there’s still the SARS markings on this contact wire inside the oven while they were melting it.
[GOVAN]: That is what you’re looking for?
[JOHAN]: That is what we’re looking for and that is 100% evidence for us that this is not legit.

[GOVAN]: The team waits on final clearance from law enforcement - three hours lost before the operation gets going..

UPSOUND TRAVELING
[SUB GOVAN]: Hey! They're delaying you.

[GOVAN]: Let's stay back with the camera.
[COP]: Hey! Come open here!

[GOVAN]: Why are the police inside there? This is not what we expected to find.


[JOHAN]: The information and the intelligence that we do on that one the place, like I said, we are watching this place for maybe two three years already.

[GOVAN]: How you Sir, I’m Govan from Carte Blanche.
[SINGH]: [inaudible] Mr. Singh
[GOVAN]: Mr. Singh, do you melt hot copper?
[SINGH]: NO! Ha! No, it’s because this is what, this is OR and that is the material what we….

[GOVAN]: The team sweeps through the property fast - every corner, even the furnace.

[JOHAN]: At this stage only aluminium that's in the furnace. But we must just go through the premises and see maybe we find copper.

[GOVAN]: For a foundry of its size, the place is unusually quiet.

[GOVAN]: So one, one of our camera guys has found a… what appears to be an underground furnace.

[GOVAN]: It's still hot. What were you burning?
[SINGH]: We make ingots, we don’t deal with hot copper, sir. We don’t deal with copper, sir.

[GOVAN]: He explains the furnace waste is reworked into solid blocks.

As the search wraps up - no large scale copper has been found. And that marked police car we spotted earlier? Turns out, it was local cops apparently running their own second-hand goods check.

[GOVAN]: So what do you think is happening?
[JOHAN]: I don't know, I think everything is not in order yet. I don't think everything is legit. I think they are lucky that we just might come on the wrong time.
[GOVAN]: We didn’t find anything?
[JOHAN]: We didn't find anything, unfortunately.
[GOVAN]: Does that happen?
[JOHAN]: That's happens. We had a 50/50 chance. Better luck next time.

[GOVAN]: While each raid chips away at the surface, the copper trade keeps running - organised, relentless, and driven by big money.



 
PROMOS
PROMO 1
[GOVAN]: They’re not stealing cables anymore - they’re taking tonnes of copper in elaborate heists.

[MISHCA]: It’s very deliberate and decisive attack. It's very premeditated and it's incredibly well set up.

[GOVAN]: Syndicates. Smelters and Silent buyers - feeding a global market worth millions.


PROMO 2

[GOVAN]: Once a petty scrap crime, copper theft has morphed into a black market worth millions.

[ROY]: To steal a ton of copper, you can put a lot of money in your pocket.

[GOVAN]: Heavily armed robbers expertly execute organized heists……. making off with truck loads of copper at a time.

[TRUCK STOP OWNER]: 20 guys came lock, stock and barrel

[GOVAN]: The copper industry is under siege.

PROMO 3
[GOVAN]: The demand for copper is huge. And criminal syndicates are stepping up to meet it.

[MICHIEL]: If there's a willing buyer, there's a guy who's willing to steal it and to make money from the business./

[GOVAN]: Targeting cargo trucks, foundries and warehouses for big pay days.


[TRUCK STOP OWNER]: Highly, highly organized. . They didn't decide to do this job a day before.

[GOVAN]: We track the evolution of the illicit copper market.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South Africa is being unplugged. We expose a shadow industry of large-scale copper heists where syndicates, smugglers and silent buyers strip the nation for profit.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: - a crime trend we've reported on before has morphed - tension in armed escourts - action in a raid
metadata.Summary: LOGLINE Copper is the lifeblood of South Africa’s infrastructure and criminals are ripping it out. This we know, this we’ve covered. But the crime trend has morphed, from live power cables and rail lines to a next level large scale criminal operations targeting cargo trucks, foundries and warehouses.
metadata.Further information: PITCH What was once petty scrap crime is now a million-rand black market feeding local syndicates and the global demand as copper theft takes on a new modus operandi. It’s not about targeting the low level thieves stealing bit by bit, it’s about closing the black market that’s honed in on big quantity thefts. This lucrative industry is now forced to have armed escorts protecting their loads in transit as syndicates shift their sights. HOW TO TELL IT We get the inside track from one of SA leading investigative companies piecing together the illicit trade in copper. They’ve got footage and rare insights into a market that has become a vicious cycle with some of the very targets, becoming the buyers. Stolen copper is often bought back by dodgy smelting facilities, getting in black market stock at a dramatically reduced price from the criminals that steal it. ELEMENTS RIDE-ALONG – THE TENSION We ride with private security teams protecting copper shipments staking out dangerous routes. We unpack the transit chain, how stolen copper moves from pylons and cable trenches to the black market, and eventually overseas, despite export bans. EXPERTISE – THE INSIGHT We’ll speak to specialist private investigators and insurers covering copper cargo worth millions, explore the threads leading to a speculative but highly plausible export economy, where stolen copper is melted, disguised, and shipped out despite official bans. FORENSICS – THE TECH The investigations include a CSI styled element - they recover fragments of cut cable, trace tool marks, lift fingerprints off truck doors, and map syndicate movements through their informer networks. RAID – THE ACTION We tag along with a team of investigators as they hit suspect smelters in search of hot copper. THE IMPACT From street-level theft to export, this crime trend is halting train networks, plunging communities into darkness, and crippling vital infrastructure. It’s not just copper that’s being stolen, it’s sabotage. It’s about national stability. Copper powers everything and right now, South Africa is being unplugged. This takes the viewer on a raw, investigative dive into the country’s illicit copper trade. KEY THEMES • The Rise of Copper Theft: What’s driving demand? • Hot Cargo: How copper is hijacked in transit, and what security teams are up against • Infrastructure Under Attack: Real-time impact on electricity, transport, and telecoms • Insured Losses, Uncounted Costs: The economics of copper theft • Where It Goes: Speculation and intelligence on export markets and supply chains ADDITIONAL CONTEXT | FIGURES FROM EXISTING RESEARCH DOCS Approximately 150 000 tonnes of copper scrap is legally traded in South Africa each year, with a value of over R10 billion. Most is sold on the local market, with a smaller percentage, approximately 13%, exported to other countries. However, some experts believe this figure may be underestimated, due to industrial-scale under-invoicing and mislabelling. Stolen copper smuggled by port leaves the country in containers that are either mislabelled or have false documentation. In some cases, scrap copper is labelled as raw copper. This practice, which involves customs fraud, appears to be common both in the smuggling of stolen copper and in the export of scrap copper by some legitimate dealers. In other cases, illegal scrap copper is mislabelled as non-metal goods, such as textiles, and then exported under the corresponding codes SHIFT FROM EXPORTING SCRAP COPPER TO RAW COPPER – POSSIBLY STOLEN The 2022 Trade and Industrial Policies Strategies report also points to a situation where, according to SARS figures, South Africa ‘now exports more raw copper than it produces and imports, and four times more than the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy reports’. With regard to stolen copper, there are no precise estimates of how much is traded, partly because some is laundered back into the legal market, making it untraceable. However, it appears more is exported than in the legal trade. INTERNATIONAL MARKET n 2021, China accounted for about 85% of all scrap metal exported from South Africa. 81 This was followed by Germany (3.24%) and India (3.21%). Other countries or regions importing South African scrap copper include Hong Kong SAR (China), the Netherlands, Korea, Belgium, Malaysia, Botswana and Lesotho THE MONEY A private investigator source has explained that a container used for export through the ports can typically hold about 24 000 kilograms of scrap copper. If it is bought at R70 per kilogram (half the current legal price) but sold at the full price of R140 per kilogram, the profit on a single container is R1.7 million The general price for scrap copper wiring ranges from R20 to R60 per kilogram.46 However, the value of stolen copper is in the lower range, usually between R15 and R20 per kilogram. After the copper has been recycled and processed, the selling price can increase to between R140 and R160 per kilogram.
